clinicalPearls: Defined as erythema and scaling affecting at least ninety per cent of the body surface, representing a dermatological emergency rather than a single diagnosis
The commonest underlying causes are pre-existing dermatoses (notably psoriasis and eczema), drug reactions, and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with a proportion remaining idiopathic
Widespread inflammation impairs the skin barrier, causing high-output fluid, protein and heat loss with a risk of hypothermia, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance
Peripheral oedema, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly may accompany the skin changes, and high-output cardiac failure can occur in vulnerable patients
Clues to the underlying cause include nail and scalp changes suggesting psoriasis, a preceding drug history, or islands of sparing and intense pruritus suggesting lymphoma
Repeated skin biopsies over time, together with blood film and lymphocyte studies, help identify Sezary syndrome and other specific causes
Secondary infection and sepsis are important complications given the disrupted barrier and thermoregulation
Management combines urgent supportive care (fluid balance, warmth, emollients and nutrition) with withdrawal of any culprit drug and treatment directed at the underlying disease
reference.pathophysiology: Erythroderma results from a massive increase in the rate of epidermal turnover and a generalised inflammatory infiltrate that together produce diffuse erythema and scaling. The widespread cutaneous vasodilatation and loss of the epidermal barrier lead to substantial transepidermal water loss, heat loss and protein loss through desquamated scale, disturbing fluid, electrolyte and temperature homeostasis. Increased cutaneous blood flow can precipitate high-output cardiac failure, while barrier failure predisposes to infection. The underlying trigger differs by cause, ranging from the amplified inflammation of an existing dermatosis or a drug hypersensitivity reaction to malignant T-cell proliferation in cutaneous lymphoma, but the shared final pathway explains the common systemic complications.
additionalDifferentials: Drug reaction, including drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and Sezary syndrome
Idiopathic erythroderma and, in neonates, inherited ichthyoses
additionalInvestigations: Serial skin biopsies to seek a specific underlying dermatosis or lymphoma
Full blood count with blood film and Sezary cell count, plus peripheral blood flow cytometry
Renal function, electrolytes, albumin and inflammatory markers to assess metabolic consequences
Comprehensive drug history and review of recently introduced medications
Assessment for lymphadenopathy and organomegaly with imaging if lymphoma is suspected
Cultures of skin and blood if secondary infection or sepsis is suspected
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability, hypothermia or high-output cardiac failure
Fluid, electrolyte and protein depletion from barrier failure
Sepsis arising from secondary skin infection
Features suggesting cutaneous lymphoma such as intense pruritus, lymphadenopathy or atypical circulating lymphocytes
A drug reaction with systemic involvement requiring immediate drug withdrawal
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and the patient's comorbidities: erythroderma from a benign dermatosis or a withdrawn drug usually settles with treatment, whereas lymphoma-associated erythroderma carries a poorer outlook, and the acute metabolic complications can be life-threatening in the elderly or frail.
pitfalls: Treating erythroderma as a diagnosis in itself and failing to search for the underlying cause
Underestimating the fluid, protein and temperature losses and the risk of high-output cardiac failure
Relying on a single non-diagnostic biopsy rather than repeating biopsies to detect lymphoma
Missing a culprit drug or overlooking secondary infection and sepsis
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on erythroderma
